newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rouble weakness sends ripple through T-bill market.
newsitem.headline: Rouble weakness sends ripple through T-bill market.

text.p: A steeper-than-usual fall in the rouble has sent ripples through the Russian Treasury bill market, making dollar investments more attractive and hampering plans to cut interest rates, analysts said on Thursday.

Dealers say the gradual easing of the rouble rate against the dollar picked up speed in August, until braked by central bank intervention late in the month. This made investors in short Treasury bills, where yields were less than 50 percent, consider looking to dollars as a safer bet, they said.
The rouble has this month been back on track, falling daily only a few points against the dollar, but some analysts says uncertainty has been sown among investors.

"The question is whether this is a permanent policy and whether the damage they did through August with the rapid devaluation policy has thrown domestic and foreign investors off," said Dirk Damrau, head of research at Renaissance Capital.
"There is still some uncertainty over what their true intentions are," he said.
Under Russia's crawling peg exchange rate policy, which runs until the end of this year, the rouble should be trading in a 5,500-6,100 per dollar corridor on December 31 this year.
Policy after this date is unclear, but the government's draft 1997 budget assumes an average exchange rate of 5,560.
The rouble was unchanged on Thursday at 5,363 to the dollar on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX).
Dealers said the central bank bought roubles on Monday and Tuesday to support the T-bill market.

"The central bank realises that banks and investors may change their attitude towards Treasury bills and prefer dollar investments. This is why it has been raising its dollar rates during the last week more slowly," an Inkombank dealer said.
On June 28, the MICEX rate was 5,105, and 5,189 on July 31. But on August 30, it was at 5,352, pointing to a steeper fall.
"Some damage was done in that the rapid compression of yields that was taking place halted and has reversed," Damrau said.
The yield on an auction of three-month T-bills on Wednesday rose to 65.77 percent from 63.18 percent on August 21.
"It is more likely for an investor to put their funds into dollars than stay in GKOs," said Albja Alliance Bank chief foreign exchange dealer Dmitry Slobodnik.
The government has said it wants to cut the yield on T-bills to between 20 and 50 percent by the end of the year.
Real interest rates in Russia are among the highest in the world. Consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in August, and officials forecast a year-on-year rate in December of about 25 percent.
The authorities hope recent moves to broaden access to the market for foreign investors will help. However, some analysts say the capped 19 percent yield for non-residents is not enough.
"There is a wide range of Bradys they can get into," Slobodnik said.

"I am sure that the central bank has enough possibilities to keep the rouble inside the corridor. They have huge reserves. But I am not sure it will be enough to get new foreign investment into GKOs," he added.

But Andrei Yashchenko, fixed income analyst at United City Bank, said the rouble's fall last month was a one-off. Rouble supply increased as a result of a relaxation in banks' compulsory reserve requirements, he said.
"It mainly went not to GKOs but to the forex market because people want to hedge their investments with stable currencies."
But he said the impact on T-bills had been limited. Yashchenko said the rouble would end the year in the middle of its permissible band against the dollar.
"We do not see any prospects for any further depreciation of the rouble. There are no macro-economic indicators which could lead to this situation," he said.
"We may even expect a slight appreciation by the end of the year due to foreign investment coming to the Russian economy."
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
